passages.original: plerique enim uaria senserunt, uti Critias et eius discipuli sanguinem esse animam dicentes, istam utique animam, qua uiuimus, quae est sensibilis, non illam animam, quae rationabilis et intellegibilis interioris hominis aestimatur. Hippocrates autem etsi Critiae non inprobauit ingenium nec disputationem eius redarguit, tamen sententiae non adquieuit. Aristoteles endelechiam dixit, ignem alii esse uoluerunt. nos igitur huiusmodi diuisionem teneamus, ut separemus quod est rationabile animae, cuius substantia diuinus est spiritus, sicut ait scriptura: quia insufflauit in faciem eius spiritum uitae, esse autem in ea nutrimentum quoddam uitale, quo hoc corpus animatur, esse etiam delectabile.
passages.english: For very many have held various views, as Critias and his disciples, who say that the soul is blood, meaning of course that soul by which we live, which is the sensitive [soul], not that soul which is reckoned to be the rational and intelligible [soul] of the inner man. Hippocrates, however, although he did not disapprove of Critias' ingenuity nor refute his argument, nevertheless did not acquiesce in his opinion. Aristotle called it *endelechia* [continuous actuality]; others held that it is fire. Let us, then, keep to a division of this kind: that we separate what is rational in the soul, whose substance is the divine Spirit, as Scripture says, "for he breathed into his face the breath of life," and [hold] that there is in it also a certain vital nourishment, by which this body is animated, and that there is also [a part that is] pleasure-seeking.
passages.notes: *endelechia*: Aristotle's term is usually *entelecheia*; Ambrose, following a Ciceronian tradition, uses the form *endelechia* ("continuity"). "Delectabile" here refers to the appetitive or pleasure-feeling part of the soul, as the following context shows; the rendering "pleasure-seeking" is interpretive.
